abstract.p: Mammalian PIEZO proteins (PIEZO1 and PIEZO2) act as essential mechanosensitive channels. PIEZO1 is thought to be selectively activated by Yoda molecules (Yoda1 and Yoda2). Although a molecular mechanism for PIEZO1 activation by Yoda1 exists, the origin of Yoda1 selective agonism remains obscure. Here, using electrophysiology and calcium imaging in transfected cells, we show that Yoda1 agonizes PIEZO2 but with a distinct efficacy profile compared to PIEZO1. Yoda1 increases single channel open probability and macroscopic stretch sensitivity of PIEZO2 currents as efficaciously as reported for PIEZO1, but it elicits weak PIEZO2-dependent calcium influx in absence of external stimulus, an effect detectable only under non-physiological conditions. Yoda1 slows down inactivation of indentation-evoked PIEZO2 currents, but to a lower extent compared to PIEZO1. The Yoda1 analog Dooku1, which does not modulate PIEZO1, slows down PIEZO2 inactivation similarly to Yoda1. Two PIEZO1 agonists unrelated to Yoda1 but thought to populate the same binding site in PIEZO1 have no effect on PIEZO2 inactivation, suggesting that their PIEZO1 selectivity is better than Yoda1. PIEZO2 inactivation is also modulated by Yoda1 potent analog Yoda2. Using mutagenesis and molecular dynamics simulations, we show that Yoda2 benzoic acid group forms a transient salt bridge with a conserved arginine in the Yoda binding site (R1724/R2029 in mouse PIEZO1/PIEZO2), explaining the higher potency of this analog for both channels. Together, our study re-evaluates the PIEZO1 selectivity of Yoda molecules and highlights a complex modulatory landscape toward distinct functional properties of PIEZO channels.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: PIEZO proteins encompass a small family of mechanically-activated and cation-selective ion channels exclusively present in eukaryotic organisms, with only two vertebrate members called PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 (1, 2). PIEZO channels share the same homotrimeric organization, that of a central ion conducting pore surrounded by three curved blade-like domains, each of these blades consisting of a juxtaposition of nine transmembrane helical bundles (called repeats A-I, or transmembrane helical units 9-1) (3-6). The inherent curvature of the PIEZO blades gives these proteins an overall bowl shape that deforms the surrounding membrane beyond the channel-membrane boundary (7-9). Mechanical membrane deformations such as lateral stretch or outward bending promote flattening of the PIEZO blades (10, 11), a conformational change thought to promote opening of the central pore (12-15).

PIEZO1 is expressed in many cell types, whereas PIEZO2 is mainly present in peripheral mechanosensory neurons as well as a discrete number of non-neuronal cells such as muscle and vascular endothelial cells (2, 16, 17). Genetic studies in which Piezo1 and/or Piezo2 genes have been invalidated globally or in specific tissues have revealed numerous biological roles mediated by PIEZO channels, ranging from somatovisceral mechanosensation (18-21) and proprioception (22, 23), to the growth and development of musculo-skeletal (24, 25), cardiac (26), lymphatic (27, 28) and vascular tissues (29, 30). To date, PIEZO channels have been associated with numerous ailments including blood disorders (31-34), mechanical allodynia (35-37), generalized lymphatic dysplasia (38, 39), Prune Belly syndrome (40) and abnormal musculoskeletal development (41-47).

The considerable impact of PIEZO channels on health and diseases has sparked the search for homolog-selective pharmacological modulators, both as molecular probes to dissect homolog-specific biological functions and as potential drugs to treat PIEZO-related pathologies. In this context, Yoda1, a synthetic small molecule proposed to act as a PIEZO1-specific agonist, has been discovered from a high-throughput screening campaign (48). Since its discovery, Yoda1 and its more potent analog Yoda2 (49) have been extensively used as a tool to unravel novel PIEZO1 functions in immune cells (50), bones (51-53), cancer progression (54, 55), and in the vascular system (56-59). In contrast to the common belief that Yoda1 and Yoda2 molecules act as highly PIEZO1-selective modulators, we show here that they can also agonize PIEZO2. These results show the relative promiscuity of these compounds and may prompt reinterpretation of some prior studies.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Yoda1 exerts distinct measurable effects when used at micromolar concentrations to PIEZO1-expressing cells: 1) it evokes spontaneous (i.e., without external mechanical stimulation) calcium influx; 2) it reduces the minimal force (activation threshold) required to measure ionic currents evoked by gigaseal pressurization (stretch currents) or by cellular indentations (poking currents); 3) it slows down inactivation and deactivation kinetics of macroscopic currents; and 4) it increases single channel open probability under steady-state membrane stretch conditions (48, 60, 61). The prevailing notion that Yoda1 acts as a PIEZO1 selective modulator mainly arose from Yoda1’s inability to elicit spontaneous calcium influx and to slow down inactivation kinetics of poking currents in PIEZO2-expressing cells (48). The effect of Yoda1 on PIEZO2 stretch currents has not been tested to our knowledge, perhaps because PIEZO2 was thought to be insensitive to membrane stretch until recently (15, 62, 63).

sec.title: Yoda1 robustly modulates PIEZO2 stretch currents
sec.p: We first tested the ability of Yoda1 to modulate PIEZO2 stretch currents. Mechano-insensitive HEK293TΔPZ1 cells (38) were transfected with a plasmid encoding mouse PIEZO2 and measured the next day to capture single channel currents in presence of 20 µM Yoda1 or vehicle control (0.05% dimethyl sulfoxide, or DMSO) at a constant patch pressure of -60 mmHg (Figure 1a). The pipette potential was held at +60 mV, establishing a membrane potential near -90 mV to increase the amplitude of single-channel events (60). Idealization of these currents reveal that Yoda1 increases PIEZO2’s mean open time from 16.6 ± 1.7 ms to 39.7 ± 5.4 ms (two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test p-value < 0.0001) while decreasing PIEZO2’s mean shut time from 383 ± 66 ms to 232 ± 43 ms (two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test p-value = 0.0006) (Figure 1b). Similar reciprocal microscopic effects of Yoda1 have been reported for PIEZO1 (60). Dividing the mean open time by the sum of mean open and shut times yielded open probability values that clearly increased in the presence of Yoda1, from 0.06 ± 0.01 to 0.17 ± 0.03 (Mann-Whitney U test p-value = 0.0021) (Figure 1c). A similar Yoda1-induced change in open probability was previously observed for PIEZO1 stretch currents (60). Dwell time analysis of single channel currents reveals that PIEZO2 populates at least three distinct open and shut states with distinct exponential lifetimes, all of them being reciprocally modulated by Yoda1 (Figure 1d), as previously observed for PIEZO1 (60). Two to three days after transfection, we next measured macroscopic PIEZO2 stretch currents evoked by brief suction pulses of incremental amplitude from +5 to -165 mmHg (Figure 1e). Fitting the relative amplitude of peak currents (I/Imax) using a Boltzmann function indicates that the presence of Yoda1 in the patch pipette correlates with a shift of the mid-point pressure (i.e, pressure needed to reach half of maximal activation, or P1/2) by about +20 mmHg (-55.4 ± 5.3 vs. -36 ± 4.5 mmHg, Mann-Whitney U test p-value = 0.0117), similar to the reported +15/20 mmHg shift for PIEZO1’s P1/2 value (48, 61). These results show overall that Yoda1 potentiates PIEZO2 stretch currents to a similar extent as reported for PIEZO1 (48, 60).

sec.title: Yoda1 can spontaneously activate PIEZO2, but only under non-physiological conditions
sec.p: Given the strong modulation of PIEZO2 stretch currents by Yoda1, we sought to re-evaluate the ability of this molecule to elicit spontaneous calcium influx in PIEZO2-expressing cells, i.e, in absence of external mechanical stimulation. Two distinct scenarios could explain why this effect has not been previously observed. First, the ability of Yoda1 to modulate mechanically-evoked PIEZO2 currents (measured electrophysiologically) and to spontaneously activate PIEZO2 (measured using calcium imaging) could be mediated by distinct pharmacological mechanisms, as recently suggested for PIEZO1 (64). On the other hand, the activatory effect of Yoda1 on PIEZO2 might be too weak to be detected in absence of external mechanical stimulus, likely due to PIEZO2’s inherently higher mechanical activation threshold (15, 62).

To tease out these scenarios, we sought to test if an activatory effect can be detected by increasing the amplitude of calcium signals. To this aim, we used an isotonic “calcium boosted solution” (CBS) containing 30 mM calcium, low potassium, and no sodium, to increase the inward electrochemical driving force for calcium ions and eliminate competitive permeants (see Materials and Methods). We transfected HEK293TΔPZ1 cells with a control plasmid encoding the calcium-sensitive fluorescent reporter GCaMP6m (GC6) (65), or with bicistronic plasmids encoding mouse PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 together with GC6 (61). One minute after Yoda1 perfusion, transfected cells were exposed to the calcium ionophore ionomycin to normalize maximal calcium signals (maxΔF/F0) as a function of the maximal GC6 response (to compensate for variability in GC6 plasmid expression).

In the presence of physiological saline (Hank’s Balanced Salt Solution, HBSS), Yoda1 failed to yield detectable PIEZO2 activation whereas it robustly activated PIEZO1 (Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn’s multiple comparison correction p-values 0.4253 vs. <0.0001, respectively) (Figure 2a). In contrast, in the presence of CBS, Yoda1 was able to activate both channels (Kruskal-Wallis tests with Dunn’s multiple comparisons p-values <0.0001 for both PIEZO1 and PIEZO2). We noticed that, for unclear reasons, application of DMSO alone tends to evoke small calcium transients in PIEZO2 transfected (Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn’s multiple comparison correction p-values = 0.2484 in HBSS and 0.0022 in CBS), but not PIEZO1-transfected (p-values > 0.9999) cells. This effect could be due to a weaker expression of GC6, evidenced by the overall lower absolute magnitude of ionomycin-dependent fluorescence signals in these cells (this would amplify the ionomycin-normalized amplitude of a small perfusion artefact) (Figure 2a). Nevertheless, because this effect is small compared to Yoda1’s, it does not invalidate the conclusion that Yoda1-induced PIEZO2 activation can be detected in absence of external mechanical stimulus, albeit under extreme, non-physiological ionic environment.

sec.p: The PIEZO2 structure was recently shown to adopt the characteristic flattened conformation associated with an open state (15) in response to hypertonic, but not hypotonic shocks (66). This seemed counterintuitive since PIEZO1 flattened under hypotonic, but not hypertonic conditions. This conundrum was elegantly explained by the unique property of PIEZO2 to interact with the cytoskeletal-associated protein filamin-B, altering PIEZO2’s response to distinct mechanical stimuli (66). Based on these recent findings, we next sought to test if extracellular hypertonicity and Yoda1 could act synergistically. We compared the amplitude of Yoda1-induced calcium signals (normalized to DMSO vehicle control) in cells transfected with our PIEZO2-IRES-GC6 plasmid under isotonic (1X HBSS) or hypertonic (2X and 3X HBSS) conditions. The amplitude of calcium signals were approximately 2- to 3-fold larger in hypertonic vs. isotonic conditions (Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s multiple comparisons p-values = 0.0119 and <0.0001 for 2X and 3X, respectively), suggesting a larger Yoda1 activatory effect in hypertonic conditions (Figure 2b). Last, we destabilized actin polymerization with cytochalasin D prior addition of Yoda1. This treatment allowed us to detect a faint but significant PIEZO2-dependent activatory effect of Yoda1 in normal ionic conditions (cytochalasin D vs. vehicle: Mann-Whitney U test p-values <0.0001 for PIEZO2-expressing cells, but 0.3877 for control cells) (Figure 2c).

sec.title: Yoda1 modulation of PIEZO2 poking currents
sec.p: Although Yoda1 was previously found unable to modulate PIEZO2 poking currents kinetics, this conclusion was based on a small sample size (48). We recorded PIEZO2 poking currents from transfected cells, either in the presence of 20 µM Yoda1 or a vehicle control (unpaired experiments). As previously observed, PIEZO2 currents display little to no inactivation when elicited by suction pulses (Figure 1e) (62), but robustly inactivate when elicited by indentations (Figure 3a) (2). When evoked with a 5 µm poke, PIEZO2 currents inactivate about 2-fold slower in the presence of Yoda1 (two tailed Mann-Whitney U test p-value < 10-5). For comparison, PIEZO1 poking currents inactivate 5-10-fold slower in the presence of Yoda1 under similar experimental conditions (48, 60). We did not detect a change in peak current amplitude (p-value = 0.514), nor in the channel activation threshold (non-significant differences at all tested poking distances) (Figure 3a-b).

sec.p: Yoda1 is thought to act as an allosteric positive modulator by binding a hydrophobic pocket sandwiched between PIEZO1 repeats A and B, promoting flattening of the mechanosensory blade domains (61, 64, 67-69). This pharmacological mechanism was initially proposed through engineering a PIEZO1/2 chimera in which a specific amino acid sequence overlapping this binding region (corresponding to mouse PIEZO1 residues 1961-2063) is swapped with its mouse PIEZO2 homologous counterpart (61). This chimera was not modulated by Yoda1 when tested using stretch current protocols, an observation which now seems odd, given the present observations that PIEZO2 stretch currents are similarly modulated by Yoda1 (Figure 1e). To complete our electrophysiological characterization, we sought to test an effect of Yoda1 in this chimera using a protocol giving the highest detection sensitivity. To this aim, we used a pairwise protocol with brief poke stimuli to measure deactivation kinetics, the most Yoda1-sensitive gating parameter known for PIEZO1 (60). Deactivation kinetics in this chimera is completely insensitive to 30 µM Yoda1 (p-value = 0.1567), in contrast to wild-type PIEZO1 in which it robustly slows down (paired t-test p-value = 0.0171) (Figure 3c). This chimera is, therefore, definitely insensitive to Yoda1.

sec.title: Modulation of PIEZO2 poking currents by other small molecules
sec.p: The replacement of Yoda1’s pyrazine ring for a benzoic acid group led to the creation of Yoda2, an improved analog which agonizes PIEZO1 at nanomolar concentrations (49). We thus sought to test if Yoda2 modulates PIEZO2 currents with similar potency. Although the effect of Yoda1 on PIEZO2 is larger when probed using stretch currents, we used PIEZO2 poking currents instead because these currents are quicker to measure, facilitating the construction of dose-response curves along a range of concentrations. Using this approach, we found that Yoda2 slows down PIEZO2 inactivation kinetics at nanomolar concentrations, with a half maximal effective concentration (EC50) about one order of magnitude lower compared to Yoda1 (∼0.4 vs. ∼10 µM, Figure 4a-b). At saturating concentrations, however, Yoda2 exerts a smaller effect than Yoda1 (lower maximal efficacy). A similar efficacy difference between Yoda1 and Yoda2 has been reported for PIEZO1, as Yoda2 was shown to slow down PIEZO1 poking currents inactivation kinetics by 1.5-2-fold at saturating concentrations (64), while Yoda1 reportedly slows down inactivation of the same currents by 5-10 fold (Figure 4 Supplement 1) (60).

sec.p: Next, we tested whether other small molecules could modulate PIEZO2 poking currents, including Dooku1 (a Yoda1 analog that antagonizes the effect of Yoda1 with no known modulatory effect on PIEZO1) and two Yoda1-unrelated PIEZO1 chemical activators (named Cmpd15 and Cmpd64) identified from a structure-guided virtual screening campaign (70, 71). Unexpectedly, Dooku1 slows down inactivation of PIEZO2 poking currents by about 2-3-fold, i.e, similar to Yoda1 (Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s correction p-value <10-5) (Figure 4c). On the other hand, these currents were not significantly modulated by Cmpds 15 and 64 in our tested conditions (p-values = 0.3223 and 0.0689, respectively), suggesting that these two Yoda-unrelated activators have better PIEZO1-selectivity than Yoda molecules.

sec.title: A conserved arginine is required for Yoda2’s nanomolar potency
sec.p: The Yoda binding region is well conserved between the two channel homologs, both at the level of the backbone structure and of amino acid sequence (Figure 5a) (3-6). It thus seems reasonable to speculate that Yoda molecules modulate PIEZO2 by binding the same region. The intracellular side of this binding region possess two conserved arginine residues, R1724 and R2098 in mouse PIEZO1, which could electrostatically interact with Yoda2’s negatively-charged benzoic acid group, potentially contributing to its higher potency relative to Yoda1 (Figure 5b). Although Yoda1 is electrically neutral, virtual molecular docking studies suggest that mouse PIEZO1 R2098 interacts with Yoda1’s pyrazine group (72-74).

sec.p: We tested a pharmacological role for these basic residues in mouse PIEZO1 by substituting them for serine (to conserve their polar character while eliminating their positive charge) and evaluated the impact of these mutations on Yoda1 and Yoda2 dose-response using calcium imaging (Figure 5c, left panels). We fitted these dose-response curves with a standard binding equation and extracted their EC50 values. To ease comparison between mutants and WT channels, we normalized the mutants’ EC50 value to that obtained for WT PIEZO1 and plotted normalized EC50 for both Yoda1 and Yoda2 and for each mutant (Figure 5c, right panel). Clearly, the R2098S mutation has no effect on the potency of either Yoda1 or Yoda2, as the normalized EC50 obtained for both molecules is close to unity, ruling out a functional electrostatic interaction involving R2098. In contrast, the R1724S mutation reduces Yoda2 potency about 4-fold relative to WT, with little to no effect on Yoda1 potency (Yoda1 vs. Yoda2: two tailed Mann-Whitney U test p-value = 0.034). The large reduction of Yoda2’s potency in the R1724S mutant suggests that R1724 stabilizes Yoda2 by forming a salt bridge.

sec.title: Yoda2 forms a transient salt bridge in the Yoda binding site
sec.p: The side chain of R1724 displays different orientations in different PIEZO1 experimental structures (Figure 6a). To quantify this orientation, we calculated the pseudo-dihedral torsion angle between the center of the guanidinium group (R1724-Cζ) and three reference atoms (Figure 6b). We next evaluated the temporal distribution of this torsion angle from our recent multiscale simulations of full-length PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 (15). Our analysis reveals that this side chain populates two major rotamer orientations, one with torsion angles of 50-100° and the other with torsion angles around -80°. A similar torsion angle distribution can be detected across nine PIEZO1 experimental structures (Figure 6 Supplement 1a). Critically, rotamers with torsion angles around -80° point the guanidinium group towards the Yoda binding site, while the other rotamers point this group away from it.

sec.p: To explore in more detail how the orientation of the guanidinium group of this conserved arginine affects Yoda2 binding, we performed three replicas of all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of a Yoda2 molecule bound to the Yoda binding site in both PIEZO1 and PIEZO2. Instead of a full-length model, we used a truncated blade (which include Repeats A-C, the anchor region and the intracellular beam) obtained from open state models for both channels. Overall, Yoda2 populates stable binding poses near the intracellular side of the Yoda binding site in both channels, similar to Yoda1 in PIEZO1 (68) (Figure 6c-d, Figure 6 Supplements 1b-c and 2). Our analysis reveals a clear correlation between the torsion angle and the formation of a salt-bridge between Yoda2 and the conserved arginine (R1724/R2029 in mouse PIEZO1/2). This bridge is stable for torsion angle values around -80° and become destabilized when R1724 or R2029 populate rotamers with positive torsion angles. In its dominant binding pose, Yoda2 also forms several non-covalent interactions with surrounding side chains in the Yoda binding site (Figure 6c-d).

The conserved arginine in the Yoda binding site (R1724/R2029 in mouse PIEZO1/2) also electrostatically engages with an endogenous glutamate residue (E1688/E1993 in mouse PIEZO1/2) (Figure 6 Supplement 3). In our previous full-length simulations, this endogenous salt bridge appears mainly in only one subunit (10 out of 13 replicas), likely because this conserved arginine is highly mobile, preventing the formation of a long-lasting bridge (Figure 6 Supplement 4a-b). In our all-atom simulations, the conserved arginine R1724/R2029 is closer to Yoda2’s benzoic group than E1688/E1993’s carboxy group (Figure 6 Supplement 4c-d), suggesting that Yoda2 is able to displace an loose endogenous salt bridge by substituting a glutamate side chain by its benzoic group.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Since its discovery, Yoda molecules have been used as selective PIEZO1 activators to unravel biological functions of this important mechanotransduction channel. Yet, we show here that these molecules also agonize PIEZO2, albeit with a drastically different efficacy profile. Indeed, while Yoda1 positively modulates stretch currents to a similar extent for both homologs, Yoda1 and Yoda2 only moderately slow down inactivation of PIEZO2 poking currents. Yoda1 also fails to evoke spontaneously PIEZO2-dependent calcium influx, unless the cells were osmotically stressed, their actin cytoskeleton destabilized, or their external ionic environment manipulated to favor calcium entry.

We also discovered that Dooku1, a Yoda1 analog with no effect on PIEZO1 (60, 68, 71), was able to modulate PIEZO2 inactivation of poking currents similarly to Yoda1, suggesting that this molecule could be optimized to create a PIEZO2 selective agonist. On the other hand, we show that compounds 15 and 64, two rationally identified PIEZO1 agonists (68), have no modulatory effect on PIEZO2 inactivation of poking currents. Future work will be needed to confirm whether these molecules have no modulatory effects on other functional properties of PIEZO2, in which case these molecules could represent promising PIEZO1 activators with better selectivity.

Our results further show that Yoda2 binds with a similar pose in both channels computationally captured in their flat/open conformation. In this binding pose, Yoda2’s benzoic acid group engages the guanidinium group of a conserved arginine in the Yoda binding site (R1724/R2029 in mouse PIEZO1/PIEZO2) to form an electrostatic salt bridge. We propose that the formation of this bridge, even transient, increases Yoda2’s binding affinity relative to Yoda1, enabling the detection of agonist effects at nanomolar concentrations. This work thus opens new avenues for drug design and optimization.

What molecular mechanisms could explain the different efficacy profile of Yoda molecules against PIEZO1 and PIEZO2? One possible culprit for Yoda1’s inability to evoke robust calcium influx through PIEZO2 could be its inherently high pressure-threshold for activation (62, 75). In the presence of Yoda1, PIEZO2’s activation threshold would remain higher than the resting membrane tension of the cell, limiting the frequency of spontaneous opening. Alternatively, since Yoda1 was proposed to use two distinct binding poses for spontaneous activation and current modulation of mechano-currents (64), Yoda1 may fail to occupy the proper binding pose necessary for channel activation in PIEZO2. The lower efficacy of Yoda molecules on PIEZO2 poking currents inactivation kinetics could be due to distinct interactions with cytoskeletal and adhesion proteins known to modulate inactivation kinetics of poking currents (66, 76, 77). Future studies will be needed to understand the origin of the differential pharmacological profile Yoda molecules exert on mammalian PIEZO homologs.

Our study suggests that certain roles attributed to PIEZO1 using Yoda1 in vivo or in cellulo could actually be contributed (at least partly) by PIEZO2 (especially if endogenous mechanical forces were present). For instance, reducing PIEZO2 expression in cells that co-express PIEZO1 also reduces the effect of Yoda1 (49, 78, 79). Although it is unclear whether PIEZO1 expression was reduced in these cells, this observation could be reconciled assuming a PIEZO2 contribution to the effect of Yoda1. Along the same line, since Yoda1 was shown to increase the expression of the lymphatic valve gene ITGA9 in a PIEZO1-independent manner (27), this genetic effect could be mediated by PIEZO2, which is also present in lymphatic endothelial cells (80).

Some reported effects of Yoda1 could also be mediated by proteins unrelated to the PIEZO channel family. For example, Yoda1 was recently shown to inhibit Kv1.3 (81), a major potassium channel in immune cells. Since Yoda1 was shown to modulate certain inflammatory responses, these immunological effects could be mediated independently of PIEZO channel activation, for instance through Kv1.3 inhibition (82-84). Lastly, Yoda1 was shown to induce phosphorylation of protein kinase B (Akt) and extracellular-related kinases (ERK) 1 and 2 in vascular endothelial cells (85) in the presence of GsMTx4, a spider toxin which inhibits mechanosensitive channels including PIEZO1 and 2 (86-88).

We previously engineered a Yoda1-insensitive PIEZO1/2 chimera based on the assumption, now obsolete, that PIEZO2 is insensitive to Yoda1 (61). We show here that this chimeric swap (swapping mouse PIEZO1 residues 1961-2063 for their homologous mouse PIEZO2 counterparts) completely abolishes Yoda1’s ability to modulates channel kinetics, further strengthening the conclusion that this construct is fully insensitive to this agonist.

How could Yoda1 modulate ionic currents in both wild-type channels, but not in this chimera? In this construct, only about half of the residues forming the Yoda1 binding site (residues contained within repeat A) are swapped, implying that the chimera’s Yoda binding site is hybrid, contributed by residues from both PIEZO1 and PIEZO2. Amongst the 102 residues encompassed in this chimeric region, 21 are not conserved, meaning that this hybrid site has a different amino acid composition than in either channel. These chemical differences may allosterically modulate ligand binding affinity and/or efficacy, resulting in a weaker binding, in a binding with different, non-efficacious poses (64), or in binding poses with similar affinities between flat (open) and curved (closed) conformations, resulting in silent (non-efficacious) binding (68, 69). Further computational studies will be needed to explore these possibilities.

sec.title: Molecular cloning
sec.p: We used plasmids encoding mouse PIEZO1 (pCDNA3.1-mPIEZO1) and (PIEZO2Sport6-mPIEZO2), gifted earlier by Ardèm Patapoutian (Scripps Research). The bicistronic plasmids pCDNA3.1-mPIEZO1-IRES-GCaMP6m and pCDNA3.1-mPIEZO2-IRES-GCaMP6m were created in-house earlier (61). mPIEZO1 single point mutations were created and sequence-verified by Epoch Life Science using a pMO-mPIEZO1 plasmid.

sec.title: Cell culture, transfection and reagents
sec.p: HEK293TΔPZ1 cells (gifted earlier from Ardèm Patapoutian), were cultured at 37°C and 5% CO2 in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (GIBCO) supplemented with Penicillin-Streptomycin and 5% fetal calf serum (Life technologies). HEK293TΔPZ1 cells grown in 12 well plates coated with Matrigel at a 1/50 dilution (Corning), were transfected as previously described with slight modifications (89): 3 μg of mPIEZO2 plasmid or 1 μg PIEZO1 plasmid were transfected to 90% confluent HEK293TΔPZ1 cells in a one well of a 12 well plate. Yoda1 (Millipore-Sigma), Yoda2 (Tocris), Dooku1 (Tocris), Cmpd15 (Chembridge chemical ID:7410103), Cmpd64 (Chembridge chemical ID:33734878), and Cytochalasin D (Millipore-Sigma) were dissolved as stock solutions in pure DMSO (Millipore-Sigma) at 40, 40, 10, 30, 30, and 2 mM, respectively. At the time of experiments, compounds were diluted to desired concentrations by dilution in the indicated solutions followed by 10-15 s vortexing. For calcium imaging experiments, compounds were extemporaneously added by manual pipetting to the cell wells.

sec.title: Electrophysiology
sec.p: For single channel recordings, transfected cells were re-seeded on glass coverslips coated with Matrigel at a 1/50 dilution (Corning) one day after transfection and immediately used. Patch pipettes were pulled from G150F borosilicate capillaries (Warner Instruments) a P-97 puller (Sutter Instrument) and heat-polished using a Microforge-MF2 (Narishige), yielding a resistance of 3-5 MΩ. Single channel currents were elicited using gigaseal pressurization (high-speed pressure clamp, ALA Scientific) in HBSS (Thermofisher), acquired using an Axopatch 200B amplifier and an analog-digital converter Digidata 1550B (Molecular Devices) as individual 1 min continuous gap-free recordings using a sampling rate of 500 kHz and a filtering frequency of 5 kHz. Data were subsequently filtered at 500 Hz for display. Single channel time series were idealized using Clampfit using a dead time of 10 µs. A MATLAB (MathWorks, USA) script posted to Github (https://github.com/LacroixLaboratory) was used to ignore events with duration shorter than 0.05 ms and with change of current amplitude < 25% of the preceding event.

For macroscopic recordings, re-seeded cells were used 2-3 days after transfection. Patch pipettes were pulled to a resistance of 2-3 MΩ, and currents were acquired at 50 KHz with no post-filtering. Blunt glass probes were created by fire-polishing the tip of glass pipettes to 2-4 µm. The poking probe was angled at ∼70 ° and mounted onto a piezoelectric actuator (P-841, Physik Instrumente) controlled by Clampex via an amplifier (E-625, Physik Instrumente). Before each experiment, the probe was slowly moved until visual deformation of the cell. The probe was then retracted approximately by 1 µm to set the initial probe position as close as possible to the cell surface. For inactivation/deactivation measurements, a 15 second interval was maintained between stimuli to allow for complete channel recovery (60). Inactivation time constants (Tau) were calculated by fitting the decaying phase (peak to 200 ms after peak) of the macroscopic currents with a standard mono-exponential equation in Clampfit 11.2 (Molecular Devices). Dose response curves were fitted using a default dose response equation in OriginPro: Tau = A1+A2−A11+10(LOGx0−x)p\begin{document}$A_{1}+\frac{A_{2}-A_{1}}{1+10^{\left(L O G_{x 0}-x\right) p}}$\end{document}; where A1 and A2 respectively represent the bottom and top asymptotic Tau values (A2 > A1); p represents the slope of the sigmoid curve (p > 0), x is the ligand concentration; and LOGx0 represents the ligand concentration at which Tau = A1+A22\begin{document}$\frac{A_{1}+A_{2}}{2}$\end{document}

sec.title: Calcium imaging
sec.p: Cells were washed and incubated for at least 30 min in HBSS prior measurements. The CBS solution contains 1 mM KCl, 30 mM CaCl2, 1 mM MgSO4, 108 mM N-Methyl-D-Glucosamine chloride, and 10 mM HEPES. The pH was adjusted to 7.4 with HCl and has an osmolarity of 288 mOsmol/L (all chemicals were purchased from Millipore-Sigma). For hypertonic treatments, 1X, 2X and 3X HBSS were prepared by dilution of a 10X commercial HBSS solution (Gibco). GCaMP6m fluorescence was recorded at 1 frame per second using a GFP/FITC filter set on an inverted Nikon Eclipse fluorescence microscope or with 488 nm laser excitation and emission detection between 500 and 550 nm on a Zeiss LSM 880 confocal microscope. Regions of interest (ROIs) were defined around individual cells, and fluorescence intensities were measured after background subtraction. Calcium responses were expressed as ΔF/F₀ = (F − F₀)/F₀, where F represents the fluorescence intensity at each time point and F₀ represents the mean baseline fluorescence intensity before compound addition. Dose-responses shown in Figure 5c were fitted using: y = BmaxCEC50+C\begin{document}$\frac{B_{\max } C}{E C 50+C}$\end{document}; where y represents ΔF/F0; C represents the ligand (Yoda1/2) concentration; and Bmax represents the saturated value of ΔF/F0 at infinite ligand concentrations.

sec.title: Statistics
sec.p: Statistical tests are indicated in figure legends and were performed using GraphPad Prism 9.

sec.title: Molecular dynamics simulations
sec.p: Docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations used a truncated all-atom open PIEZO1 (residues 1131 to 2190) (69). For PIEZO2, we used the previously published model generated by applying membrane tension of 9.3mN/m to the structure (PDB ID: 6KG7) using the PACE force field (15). A single blade of PIEZO2 (residues 1277-2467) was retained, and the PACE model was converted to all atoms for molecular docking and MD simulations. Molecular docking was performed using AutoDock Vina 1.2.3 with the docking grid defined between Repeat B (TM29– 30) and Repeat A (TM35–36) using MGLTools-1.5.6 and a grid size of 30 × 30 × 30 Å. The PIEZO1-Yoda2 and PIEZO2-Yoda2 complex system were assembled using CHARMM36m parameters for the protein, CHARMM36 parameters for POPC lipids, ions, and water molecules, and CHARMM General Force Field (CGenFF) for Yoda2. Both systems were neutralized and maintained at an ionic concentration of 150 mM KCl and solvated using TIP3P water. The simulation system dimensions and composition are summarized in Table 1. All-atom MD simulations were performed using GROMACS 2024.2 smp. We followed the input files generated by CHARMM-GUI, including six equilibration steps followed by production simulations. Energy minimization was performed using the steepest descent algorithm for 5,000 steps. Long-range electrostatic interactions were calculated using the Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) method with a real-space cutoff of 1.2 nm. Van der Waals interactions were smoothly switched off between 1.0 and 1.2 nm using a force-switch function. All hydrogen-containing bonds were constrained using the LINCS algorithm, allowing a 2 fs integration timestep. The system was equilibrated at 310.15 K using the V-rescale thermostat with separate coupling groups for the protein-ligand complex, membrane, and solvent. Semi-isotropic pressure coupling was applied using the C-rescale barostat at 1 bar with a compressibility of 4.5 × 10⁻⁵ bar⁻¹ and a relaxation time constant of 5 ps. Positional restraints were applied during equilibration to the protein backbone, lipids, and dihedral angles. Following equilibration, three independent production replicas were run from distinct equilibration conformations. For PIEZO1-Yoda2, Replica 1 was simulated for 20 µs on the Anton3 supercomputer. Whereas Replica 2 and 3 were simulated for 1.4 µs each using GROMACS. For PIEZO2-Yoda2, all three independent replicas were simulated for 1.2 µs each using by GROMACS. The 20 µs replica was run on Anton3 supercomputer by converting a 100 ns GRO file to a Desmond-compatible format using Viparr on Bridges2. The Anton3 simulation was performed using a multigrator integration scheme with a 2.5 fs timestep. Temperature was maintained using a Nose–Hoover thermostat at 310.15 K and pressure was controlled using the Martyna–Tuckerman–Klein (MTK) barostat with semi-isotropic coupling.Ligand–protein interaction analyses were performed using MDAnalysis and PLIP 2.1.0, and molecular visualization was carried out using VMD 1.9.3.

body.p: This study shows that the compound Yoda potentiates the function of the PIEZO2 channel, challenging the assumption that they selectively activate PIEZO1. This is an important finding and the evidence supporting this claim is solid. The authors have addressed the methodological and conceptual issues raised during review. Overall, this work will be of broad interest to researchers working with PIEZO channels across various biological scales.

[Editor's note: this version has been assessed by the Reviewing Editor without further input from the original reviewers. The authors have addressed the comments raised in the previous round of review.]
Summary:

In this work, T. Wijerathne et al. investigated and reported the agonistic effect of Yoda1 and Yoda2 over PIEZO2 function using patch clamp electrophysiology, Ca2+ imaging, and molecular dynamics. They find that Yoda1 sensitizes PIEZO2 to membrane tension, can induce Ca2+ influx, and decreases its inactivation to a lesser degree than it does to PIEZO1 channels. Additionally, their data shows that Yoda2 sensitizes PIEZO2 channels to membrane indentation to a greater extent, but it has a weaker effect on channel inactivation than Yoda1. Interestingly, they report that a mutation in a conserved arginine between PIEZO channels can be used to abolish PIEZO1-mediated Ca2+ flux in response to Yoda molecules. As a whole, the results presented here should be put into perspective against previous and future works involving systems where both PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 might be expressed. This is especially true for works where Yoda1 has been used as a basis for determining the absence of PIEZO2.
Strengths:

The authors use multiple techniques to investigate how Yoda molecules affect the three most important biophysical aspects of PIEZO channels that, when changed, result in pathophysiological responses: a) sensitivity to mechanical stimuli, b) Ca2+ entry, and c) channel inactivation. Lastly, they find a specific amino acid/region that could be exploited for drug design and/or development.
Summary:

This manuscript challenges the long-standing assumption that Yoda1 and Yoda2 are PIEZO1-selective activators. Using patch-clamp electrophysiology and calcium imaging in HEK293TΔPZ1 cells overexpressing PIEZO2, the authors demonstrate that Yoda1 potentiates PIEZO2 stretch-activated currents to a similar extent as PIEZO1 and slows PIEZO2 poking-current inactivation (albeit with lower efficacy). They further show that the more potent analog Yoda2 affects PIEZO2 at nanomolar concentrations and use mutagenesis and molecular dynamics simulations to propose that Yoda2's benzoic acid group forms a transient salt bridge with R1724 in the putative Yoda binding pocket, explaining its enhanced potency.
Strengths:

The authors are established Piezo/biophysics experts; the study is highly important, technically competent, and carries significant implications for the reinterpretation of prior work that used Yoda compounds as PIEZO1-selective probes.
The core finding that Yoda1 modulates PIEZO2 stretch currents is convincing and important.
Summary:

The manuscript reports that Yoda1 and Yoda2 agonize PIEZO2 in a manner similar to PIEZO1, increasing open probability and stretch sensitivity, but the mechanism underlying this sensitivity is incomplete. Mutagenesis was shown exclusively in PIEZO1, with no corresponding mutagenesis in PIEZO2, so the proposed mechanism in PIEZO2 is inferred by homology rather than directly tested. All experiments use mouse PIEZO2, and the human ortholog should be used before generalizing the proposed reinterpretation of the field.
Strengths:
The pressure-clamp electrophysiology demonstrating a shift in half-activation pressure for PIEZO2 is compelling evidence in support of the central claim.
The following is the authors’ response to the original reviews.

body.p: We have included new results, expanded our discussion, and added additional details in our Methods section.

disp-quote.p: Summary:

This manuscript challenges the long-standing assumption that Yoda1 and Yoda2 are PIEZO1selective activators. Using patch-clamp electrophysiology and calcium imaging in HEK293TΔPZ1 cells overexpressing PIEZO2, the authors demonstrate that Yoda1 potentiates PIEZO2 stretch activated currents to a similar extent as PIEZO1 and slows PIEZO2 poking-current inactivation (albeit with lower efficacy). They further show that the more potent analog Yoda2 affects PIEZO2 at nanomolar concentrations and use mutagenesis and molecular dynamics simulations to propose that Yoda2's benzoic acid group forms a transient salt bridge with R1724 in the putative Yoda binding pocket, explaining its enhanced potency.
Strengths:

The authors are established Piezo/biophysics experts; the study is highly important, technically competent, and carries significant implications for the reinterpretation of prior work that used Yoda compounds as PIEZO1-selective probes.

The core finding that Yoda1 modulates PIEZO2 stretch currents is convincing and important. However, several conceptual, methodological, and presentational issues need to be addressed before acceptance, as detailed below.
Weaknesses:

(1) The abstract states that Yoda1 potentiates PIEZO2 "as efficaciously as PIEZO1." This claim is accurate only for stretch currents and single-channel open probability, but the paper itself demonstrates important asymmetries: i) Yoda molecules slow PIEZO2 poking-current inactivation ~2-fold, versus ~5-10 fold for PIEZO1 (Figure 3b and ref #60). ii) Spontaneous Ca2+ entry via PIEZO2 requires non-physiological conditions (high extracellular Ca2+, hypertonic solutions) that are unlikely to occur in native cells. The abstract should be revised to clearly qualify where equivalence holds and where efficacy differences exist. IMO, the current wording risks overcorrecting the historical bias (PIEZO1-only) by going too far in the other direction.

body.p: We have changed our language throughout the manuscript to convey more accurately differences of Yoda agonism between the two Piezo homologs.

disp-quote.p: (2) Related concern: the PIEZO2 Ca2+ signal in Figure 2 is only detectable using a Ca2+-boosted solution (CBS ie 30 mM Ca2+). Physiological extracellular Ca2+ and cells normally do not experience sustained hypertonicity at these magnitudes. The authors should explicitly clarify that the practical implication of their findings is primarily for electrophysiological (patch-clamp) experiments and that the Ca2+ imaging caveat applies only under amplified conditions. Specifically, the authors should state that in standard Ca2+ imaging assays with physiological buffers, PIEZO2 is unlikely to confound Yoda1 results.

body.p: Agreed. As mentioned above, we have modified our wording to convey this point more clearly.

disp-quote.p: Related point: Can cytochalasin D (CytoD) restore a Yoda1-dependent Ca2+ signal in physiological saline? This would help determine whether the weak PIEZO2 response is primarily a membrane tension issue (cytoskeletal tethering) versus intrinsically lower channel expression or permeability. The authors already have tagged PIEZO1/2 constructs and could, in principle, normalize by surface expression.

body.p: We have repeated our acute pharmacological treatment in cells pre-treated with CytoD (or 0.5% DMSO vehicle control). These experiments were done in normal saline solution. We found that Yoda1 produces a very small (but significant) calcium influx in cells treated with CytoD. This result strengthens our conclusion that Yoda1 is capable of producing an activatory effect on Piezo2 in absence of external mechanical stimulation - albeit this effect is very small and only detectable in non-physiological (calcium-rich or destabilized cytoskeleton) conditions. It remains difficult to definitely conclude about why Yoda molecules exert different agonistic effects. We can only discuss possibilities. Differences in Ca2+ permeability is unlikely to contribute to this difference, as pore properties and selectivity for monovalent ions are similar between the two channels (see PMID: 39543876). Slight differences in how Yoda bind the Yoda binding region could explain why Yoda1 robustly modulates Piezo2 stretch currents but fails to produce robust calcium influx, as recent work suggests that these two agonist effects may originate from two distinct Yoda binding poses in this region (PMID: 38060566; PMID: 41402296). Piezo2’s intrinsically high threshold for stretch-activation could also represent a contributing factor, as figures 1e-f show that Piezo2’s midpoint activation pressure in the presence of Yoda1 (about -30 mmHg vs. -60 mmHg) might still be too high to enable robust Yoda-induced activation at the resting membrane tension of the cell. Since Piezo1 has been consistently shown (by us and others) to be expressed at a higher level than Piezo2 in transfected HEK293 cells (e.g., PMID: 20813920; PMID: 32227462, PMID: 37102984; PMCID: PMC13423835), we have not replicated these experiments with Piezo1. We have modified our manuscript to include these new results and discussion.

disp-quote.p: (3) The mean inactivation tau values for wild-type PIEZO2 poking currents in both DMSO and Yoda1 conditions (Figure 3b, approximately 15-40 ms range) appear substantially higher than values reported in published literature (typically 5-10 ms; eg, PMID: 20813920). This discrepancy needs to be addressed.

body.p: This discrepancy likely arises because inactivation kinetics of Piezo1 and/or 2 poking currents can be modulated by many biological and experimental variables that are difficult to control. Biological variables include membrane potential (PMID: 20813920), extracellular pH (PMID: 25561736), temperature (PMID: 35858335; PMID: 31413193), the presence of modulatory proteins (PMID: 37590348) and extracellular matrix (PMID: 28164706). Experimental variables include the mechanics of probe displacement (velocity and impact angle) and the precise positioning of the time-cursor near the peak current for exponential fitting. In addition, the decaying portion of Piezo poking currents is likely contributed by both inactivation and deactivation, as a recent study demonstrates relaxation of the poke stimulus during mechanical indentation in N2a cell (PMID: 42649207). Cellular viscoelastic properties and cytoskeletal organization are thus anticipated to dictate how fast this relaxation occurs, influencing the proportion of inactivating and deactivating currents in poking recordings. Since this point deviates from our main goal - to test an effect of Yoda on channel kinetics measured side-by-side – we prefer not to discuss it.

disp-quote.p: (4) The authors perform all MD simulations on a truncated PIEZO1 model and justify this choice by noting that the Yoda binding region is highly conserved between homologs. This is a reasonable and defensible starting point given the availability of well-validated PIEZO1 simulation set ups in their lab. A few points are nonetheless worth addressing: While PIEZO2 simulations are not strictly required, the authors are encouraged to briefly discuss whether any long-range structural differences between PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 (outside the binding site itself) could influence Yoda2 binding dynamics, particularly in light of the chimera data showing that PIEZO2 sequence in repeat A abolishes Yoda1 sensitivity. This reviewer still doesn't understand the reason behind this discrepancy despite it being acknowledged in the text.

body.p: We have now conducted three replicas of all-atom MD simulations of the Yoda2-bound PIEZO2 system. The new results show that the equivalent Arg residue in PIEZO2 (R2029) also forms a salt bridge with Yoda2, consistent with our observations from the Yoda2-bound PIEZO1 simulations. Taken together, these simulation results seem to point to the fact that Yoda molecules bind to a similar region in both PIEZO1 and PIEZO2. The lack of Yoda1-sensitivity in the chimera is quite puzzling, and we can only speculate about why. The swapped chimeric region includes 103 residues, 21 of which are non-conserved between PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 and distributed around the binding region (PMID: 29795280). These mutations could collectively and allosterically alter the binding free energy landscape in a manner that either 1) strongly reduce Yoda binding affinity or 2) equalize Yoda binding affinity for both curved and flat conformations, effectively rendering Yoda molecules silent binders (similar to how we previously described Dooku1 binding to Piezo1 PMID: 38060566).

disp-quote.p: Another MD-related comment is that three simulation replicas (which is impressive for such a big system) show markedly different salt bridge occupancy (82.6%, 49.7%, 99.8%; stated in the text). This wide variation suggests incomplete sampling in at least one replica. The authors should provide RMSD plots for ligand and protein backbone to assess convergence and possibly discuss whether the 49.7% replica represents a genuinely distinct binding mode or incomplete equilibration.

body.p: We have extended PIEZO1-Yoda2 replica #2 from 600 to 1400 nanoseconds. This replica shows that the salt-bridge turned ON and OFF during the simulation because the Arg side chain tends to flip. This flipping behavior is evident in the 20 µs Replica #1 (Figure 6c). In Figure 6-figure supplement 1, we analyzed our previous five replicas of MD simulations using the PACE force field. We show that the angle distributions indeed vary between replicas and subunits at the timescales currently affordable by MD technique for this large system. Therefore, it is not too surprising that the salt bridge occupancy differs between three all-atom simulations. We now provide RMSD of ligand and protein backbone for each Replica as Figure 6 supplement 1. The time evolution of Yoda2 binding poses across all simulation replicas are now illustrated in Figure 6-figure supplement 2, which shows that Yoda2 is mobile, yet remain stable in this overall hydrophobic binding site, consistent with our previous report (PNAS2023 PMID: 38060566). We also added all corresponding analysis of Yoda2-PIEZO2 in the same figures.

disp-quote.p: (5) The Discussion proposes that PIEZO2's weaker Ca2+ response to Yoda1 could partly reflect lower membrane expression. Since the authors already have fluorescently tagged PIEZO1 and 2 constructs, a simple fluorescence intensity comparison between the two (acknowledging it would reflect total rather than surface expression) could provide at least indirect support for this claim. Alternatively, if such a comparison is not feasible, the authors may consider removing membrane expression from the list of proposed explanations or explicitly acknowledging that this remains unsubstantiated speculation. The max poking currents may somewhat and roughly indicate the level expression difference too, if done exactly side by side.

body.p: PIEZO2 expression is known to be lower than PIEZO1 in heterologous systems (PMID: 20813920; PMID: 32227462, PMID: 37102984; PMCID: PMC13423835), hence we have not attempted to test if this was the case with our tagged constructs.

disp-quote.p: (6) The abstract or concluding remarks should highlight that Dooku1 is not PIEZO1-selective in its agonist-like action on PIEZO2, and that Cmpd15/Cmpd64 appear to be better PIEZO1-selective tools. This nuance is buried in the Results section.

body.p: We now list these results in the abstract.

disp-quote.p: (7) The authors should not cite PMID 31015490. Clearly, any work on MCC13 is confounded by the overwhelming expression of PIEZO1 (PMID: 42084270). Instead, the authors should also cite the literature from others who have clearly recorded stretch currents from PIEZO2 before the cited studies (eg, PMID: 37590348).

body.p: Agreed!

disp-quote.p: Summary:

The manuscript reports that Yoda1 and Yoda2 agonize PIEZO2 in a manner similar to PIEZO1, increasing open probability and stretch sensitivity, but the mechanism underlying this sensitivity is incomplete. Mutagenesis was shown exclusively in PIEZO1, with no corresponding mutagenesis in PIEZO2, so the proposed mechanism in PIEZO2 is inferred by homology rather than directly tested. All experiments use mouse PIEZO2, and the human ortholog should be used before generalizing the proposed reinterpretation of the field.
Strengths:
The pressure-clamp electrophysiology demonstrating a shift in half-activation pressure for PIEZO2 is compelling evidence in support of the central claim.
Weaknesses:

(1) In the single-channel recordings (Figure 1a), it's unclear how many channels were present in those patches. After applying -60 mmHg pressure, multiple channels would be activated (as seen in Figure 1e). The number of channels in the patch and their inactivation rate could significantly influence the open probability in such experiments. To overcome this, in the original Yoda1 article (Syeda, Ruhma, et al. eLife 2015), no additional pressure was used.

body.p: To clarify the confusion, we record single-channel PIEZO2 currents less than 24 hrs after transfection and record macroscopic PIEZO2 currents 2-3 days after transfection. Hence, unlike the cited study, our single and macro currents are obtained from different patches. When patching cells for single recordings, most patches do not show any mechano-currents and those that do typically show only one current level of single-channel conductance through the recording, even when the patch is highly pressurized.

disp-quote.p: Additionally, the reported open probability comparison (n=7 Yoda1 vs n=17 DMSO patches) has an SEM nearly as large as the effect itself (0.30 {plus minus} 0.11), consistent with a small number of outliers driving this. The underlying mean open and shut times are reported without any statistical test; only the derived open probability receives a p-value. Additionally, in Figure 1a, the Yoda1 condition noise is different from the control. This should be stated if noise filtering was applied and how, given that this could affect open probability analysis.

body.p: This is a fair point. We have removed two outliers and have performed statistical analysis on mean dwell times. The effect of Yoda1 is still highly significant. We have replaced current traces with two of similar noise levels. We acquired all single-channel current traces at 100kHz, filtered them at 5kHz, and displayed them at 500 Hz.

disp-quote.p: (2) The calcium imaging data in Figure 2 raise significant concerns regarding the chemical activation claim. The calcium-boosted solution (30 mM Ca2+) is not physiological and appears to be generally stressing cells rather than specifically activating PIEZO2: the control condition under CBS already shows an elevated signal, consistent with cells being unwell at this calcium concentration, and adding Yoda1 on top of this shifted baseline raises further questions about specificity rather than confirming it. Separately, it is unclear why DMSO alone produces measurable PIEZO2-associated calcium influx in HBSS, a result that is not addressed in the text. Figure 2 should clearly indicate when DMSO/Yoda1 perfusion was initiated, and y-axis labels are missing from panels A and B.

body.p: We agree and have toned down our chemical activation claim, insisting that this activation is very weak in absence of external mechanical stimulus, being only detectable under extreme, non-physiological conditions. We also re-analysed our data (and added fluorescence scale bars, thank you) showing time-course and scatter plots from the same cells in Figure 2a. We think the “bump” seen upon DMSO perfusion in PIEZO2 cells could be amplified by the low expression of GC6 in these cells. We now discuss this point in our revisions.

disp-quote.p: (3) In the poke experiments, an activation threshold should be calculated and reported, and amplitude data (e.g., peak current versus indentation depth) should be shown rather than only inactivation tau values. It is also unclear why mClover3- and N-GFP-tagged constructs were used in these experiments, since electrophysiological recording already confirms channel expression without requiring a fluorescent tag.

body.p: Valid point, we are now comparing peak currents for different poking distances. We have removed our Tau analysis for our tagged-PIEZO2 clones.

disp-quote.p: (4) For inactivation kinetics (Figure 3b), the authors use unpaired comparisons across separate cells, whereas the deactivation experiments (Figure 3c) use paired; it should be applied to the inactivation experiments as well. Deactivation kinetics for PIEZO2 itself should be shown.

body.p: These experiments have different goals which do not require using the same protocol. Deactivation kinetics experiments were used for the chimera because this parameter was shown by us to be the most sensitive to Yoda1. Hence, if a Yoda modulation exists, but is hard to detect in the chimera, using this protocol with paired samples provide us with the highest detection sensitivity. This level of sensitivity was not needed to detect an effect of Yoda1 on PIEZO2.

disp-quote.p: If the claim is that Yoda1 acts on PIEZO2 through the same mechanism proposed for PIEZO1, then a PIEZO1/2 chimera should be expected to show a corresponding effect on deactivation tau; instead, this chimera is reported as completely Yoda1-insensitive despite both parental channels being Yoda1-sensitive, as shown in this study.

body.p: This discrepancy is acknowledged in the text. We do not know why the chimera is Yoda insensitive and can only speculate at this point. Of note, one must acknowledge that this chimeric swapping introduces 21 amino acid changes (vs. WT PIEZO1) which may have profound allosteric effect on binding affinity and/or efficacy. MD studies would be useful to explore this possibility in a future study.

disp-quote.p: (5) Given that this reflects a different experimental paradigm for Yoda EC50, PIEZO1 should be included within Figure 4b. Additionally, EC50 bar plots should be present on this figure.

body.p: Showing EC50 plots here is not possible because each cell was exposed to only one dose of Yoda1 (unpaired measurements). We have included a Yoda1 dose-response curve against PIEZO1 inactivation Tau from our prior study (PMID: 35858335) for comparison as a Figure Supplement.

disp-quote.p: The inactivation time constant for PIEZO2 without Yoda1 is inconsistent across figures, below 20 ms in Figure 3b but above 20 ms in Figure 4c.

body.p: As explained above in our answer to Reviewer #2, these inconsistencies likely occur because PIEZO inactivation kinetics are susceptible to modulation by a number of biological and experimental factors that are not easily traceable, making it difficult to define absolute channel kinetics.

disp-quote.p: (6) Finally, the modeling is performed exclusively on PIEZO1, whereas the manuscript's central focus is PIEZO2. It is therefore unclear whether the proposed structural mechanism, including the basis for Yoda2's reduced efficacy on PIEZO2, can be directly extrapolated to PIEZO2.

body.p: We have now conducted three replicate all-atom MD simulations of the Yoda2-bound PIEZO2 system. The new results show that the equivalent Arg residue in PIEZO2 (R2029) also forms a salt bridge with Yoda2, consistent with our observations from the Yoda2-bound PIEZO1 simulations. However, the current simulations do not allow us to distinguish differential efficacy of Yoda2 toward PIEZO1 versus PIEZO2. The reduced efficacy of Yoda2 on PIEZO2 may instead arise from differences in its binding affinity for the open versus closed conformations, or from contributions of cellular components that are not represented in our MD simulations, such as the cytoskeleton.

disp-quote.p: Main:
(1) Adding more depth and detail to the methods section will help others replicate the findings.

body.p: Agreed.

disp-quote.p: (2) Methods: line 325. Describe the way each compound was prepared for each concentration without undissolved particles. Avoid using the phrase "as described before" in the methods section.

body.p: Compounds were dissolved in DMSO and simply diluted in recording solution at the time of experiments with vortex mixing.

disp-quote.p: (3) Figure 1B (comparison of open probability): only three points out of 7 (with Yoda1) seem outside the data range of the control (DMSO). It seems very unreliable for an agonist. Moreover, in Figure 1F, the data seem very noisy. I would suggest adding more n.

body.p: We have eliminated two outliers and reanalyzed our data, showing statistics for mean dwell times and open probability.

disp-quote.p: (4) The authors should add to the "Yoda1 activates PIEZO2 in the absence of external mechanical stimulus" section (or the methods) how perfusion of Yoda1 was applied.

body.p: We used manual pipetting.

disp-quote.p: (5) Lines 165 - 171. This part should be moved to the discussion and expanded on. Particularly since the reference they allude to comes from the same group.

body.p: This discussion part is needed to introduce the chimera experiments and thus should remain in Results.

disp-quote.p: (6) Figure 3B. The noise range of the time constants of inactivation is a lot. Specially for transfected cells. I would suggest a couple of sentences explaining why the authors think this happens.

body.p: This discussion is now included.

disp-quote.p: (7) Figure 4C. Tau inac of DMSO control seems very high when compared to others. I would suggest a couple of sentences explaining why the authors think this happens.

body.p: One difference is that DMSO concentration here is higher (0.25% vs 0.075%) to match the higher concentration of Yoda1 tested. Inactivation kinetics are subject to modulation by many parameters; hence we focus on side-by-side comparisons instead of absolute values.

disp-quote.p: (8) Line 213. Which standard binding equation? Include in the methods.

body.p: Done.

disp-quote.p: Rethink calculating the EC50 with dose responses that saturate. Figure5C. Are these absolute or relative EC50s?

body.p: EC50 of mutants are normalized to WT.

disp-quote.p: (9) Discussion: "Our discovery that Yoda1 modulates PIEZO2 stretch currents as effectively as PIEZO1's strongly suggests that some of the reported biological roles attributed to PIEZO1 using this agonist could be (at least partly) transduced by PIEZO2. For instance, our discovery seamlessly reconciles the puzzling fact that reducing PIEZO2 expression in cells that co-express PIEZO1 also reduces the effects of Yoda1 (49, 76, 77). Along." In the referenced works (49, 76, and 77) its not checked if PIEZO1 levels remain the same when PIEZO2 was knocked out. Here, the authors should discuss this possibility.

body.p: Good point!

disp-quote.p: Minor:
(1) Indicate in the figure legends, result or methods section, what the error bars represent.

body.p: Done.

disp-quote.p: (2) Indicate the p-value for Figure 1B.

body.p: Done.

disp-quote.p: (3) Figure 2. Include the ionomycin value that each group is normalized against.

body.p: We provide now vertical scale bars for all samples.

disp-quote.p: (4) Why not use PIEZO2 for the MD simulations?

body.p: Done.

disp-quote.p: Minor comments

(1) In the Abstract: The sentence "Although a structural framework for PIEZO1 activation by Yoda1 exists" may be confusing for readers outside the field. The authors may mean "mechanistic" or "computational" framework. Please clarify or reword.

body.p: We have reworded the abstract.

disp-quote.p: (2) Residue number in abstract: The abstract states "a conserved arginine in the Yoda binding site" without identifying it. Please add the residue number (R1724 in mouse PIEZO1) for clarity.

body.p: Done

disp-quote.p: (3) Figure 1 legend or in the method: recording mode and filter settings: The figure legend should explicitly state that single-channel recordings were obtained in cell-attached mode, and should report the filter frequency (kHz) and sampling rate used for idealization. This is essential for readers to evaluate dwell-time analysis.

body.p: Done, but details are in the method.

disp-quote.p: (4) Several instances throughout the text use "native" where "naïve" is clearly intended.

body.p: Corrected, thank you.

disp-quote.p: (5) The statement that PIEZO2 requires more mechanical force than PIEZO1 (~−60 vs ~−40 mmHg P1/2) should be interpreted cautiously without this information, and the authors should clarify whether pipette geometry was controlled between PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 experiments.

body.p: We have shown that PIEZO2 requires more force to be opened by membrane tension relative to PIEZO1 using MscL gating as a tension-calibration system (PMID: 41703062). Pipette geometry is consistent for each type of experiment (macroscopic or single-channel recordings). We have expanded our Methods.

disp-quote.p: (6) The finding that Dooku1slows PIEZO2 inactivation similarly to Yoda1 is striking and is currently underplayed. This raises important questions: Does Dooku1 elicit Ca2+ entry in PIEZO2-expressing cells? It could at least be discussed further in the text.

body.p: Likely not, since Yoda-induced calcium influx is very weak and requires non-physiological conditions to be detectable. But this is worth trying at some point.
